questions.question: Let $E\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and $f\colon E\to\mathbb R$. What does '$f$ is $C^1$ on $E$' require?
options: All first-order partials exist on $E$ and are continuous on $E$.
$f$ is continuous on $E$ and all first-order partials exist on $E$.
All first-order partials exist and are continuous at one point of $E$.
All first-order partials exist on $E$ and are bounded there.

questions.question: If $f$ is $C^2$ on an open set $E$, which further property must $f$ have?
options: $f$ is $C^3$ on $E$.
$f$ is a polynomial on $E$.
$f$ is bounded on $E$.
$f$ is $C^1$ on $E$.

questions.question: Let $F\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^2$ be $F(x)=(|x|,-|x|)$. Its components sum to zero. What can be said about the regularity of $F$?
options: $F$ is $C^2$, because its component sum is constant.
$F$ is not $C^1$: neither component is differentiable at $0$.
$F$ is $C^1$, because both components are continuous.
$F$ is $C^1$ but not $C^2$, because of the corner at $0$.

questions.question: For $f\colon E\to\mathbb R$ on an open set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, which condition defines '$f$ is $C^2$ on $E$'?
options: All second-order partials exist on $E$; their continuity is not required there.
The pure partials $\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_i^2}$ exist and are continuous on $E$; mixed ones may fail.
Every second-order partial, mixed ones too, exists and is continuous on $E$.
The Hessian $H_f(x)$ is a symmetric matrix at every point $x$ of $E$.

questions.question: Let $f\colon E\to\mathbb R$, where $E\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ is open. Why is openness useful when defining $C^1$ and $C^2$ on $E$?
options: Every continuous function on $E$ attains a maximum on $E$.
The partials of $f$ are automatically continuous on all of $E$.
$f$ extends continuously to the closure of $E$, boundary included.
Every point of $E$ is interior, allowing two-sided limits.

questions.question: The temperature on a metal plate is a $C^1$ function $T(x,y)$. Which behaviour does this rule out?
options: $T$ having a strict maximum at an interior point of the plate.
The rate $\partial T/\partial x$ jumping abruptly across a line on the plate.
$T$ changing at different rates in the $x$- and $y$-directions.
$\partial T/\partial x$ taking negative values somewhere on the plate.

questions.question: The function $f(x)=|x|$ is not $C^1$ on $\mathbb R$. Is it $C^1$ on the open interval $(0,\infty)$?
options: Yes: there $f(x)=x$, whose derivative $1$ is continuous.
No: failing to be $C^1$ on $\mathbb R$ means failing on every subset.
No: the corner at $0$ makes $f'$ discontinuous inside $(0,\infty)$.
Yes, but only on bounded intervals such as $(0,1)$.

questions.question: What is the largest open set on which $f(x,y)=\ln(x^2+y^2)$ is $C^2$?
options: $\mathbb R^2$
$\mathbb R^2\setminus\{(0,0)\}$

questions.question: For $f(x,y)=x^2+\sin y$, what is its Hessian $H_f(x,y)$, with entries ordered as $\begin{pmatrix}f_{xx}&f_{xy}\\f_{yx}&f_{yy}\end{pmatrix}$?
options: $\begin{pmatrix}2x&0\\0&\cos y\end{pmatrix}$
$\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&\sin y\end{pmatrix}$
$\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&-\sin y\end{pmatrix}$
$\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&-\sin y\end{pmatrix}$

questions.question: Let $f(x)=x^2\sin(1/x)$ for $x\neq0$ and $f(0)=0$. Then $f'(0)=0$ and $f'(x)=2x\sin(1/x)-\cos(1/x)$ for $x\neq0$. Is $f$ of class $C^1$ on $\mathbb R$?
options: Yes: $f$ is differentiable at every point of $\mathbb R$.
No: $f'$ exists everywhere but has no limit at $0$.
No: $f$ is not differentiable at $0$, because of the oscillation.
Yes: $f'(0)=0$ and $f$ is continuous at $0$, as required.

questions.question: All first-order partials of $f\colon E\to\mathbb R$ exist at every point of an open set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^2$. What can be concluded about $f$ in general?
options: $f$ is continuous on $E$, though perhaps not $C^1$.
$f$ is differentiable at every point of $E$.
Not even that $f$ is continuous on $E$.
$f$ is $C^1$ on $E$, since its partials exist everywhere.

questions.question: A function $f\colon\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R$ has $\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x\partial y}(0,0)=1$ and $\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y\partial x}(0,0)=-1$. What follows?
options: $f$ is not $C^2$ on any open set containing $(0,0)$.
$f$ fails to be even $C^1$ near $(0,0)$.
$f$ is not continuous at $(0,0)$.
$f$ is $C^2$ near $(0,0)$ but has a non-symmetric Hessian there.

questions.question: Let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $f\colon U\cup V\to\mathbb R$. Suppose $f$ is $C^2$ on $U$ and on $V$. What else is needed to conclude that $f$ is $C^2$ on $U\cup V$?
options: The sets $U$ and $V$ must have a nonempty intersection.
The union $U\cup V$ must be a connected open set.
The second partials must extend continuously to both boundaries.
No additional condition on the two open sets is needed.

questions.question: Let $f(x)=x^2$ for $x\ge0$ and $f(x)=ax^2+bx$ for $x<0$. For which $a,b$ is $f$ of class $C^1$ but not $C^2$ on $\mathbb R$?
options: $a=1$, with $b$ arbitrary
$b=0$ and $a\neq1$
All $a,b\in\mathbb R$

questions.question: A $C^1$ function $f$ on $\mathbb R^2$ has $f(1,2)=4$ and $\nabla f(1,2)=(3,-1)$. What does the linear approximation give for $f(1.1,\,1.9)$?
options: None: a $C^1$ function need not be differentiable.

questions.question: The function $g(x,y)=x^{7/3}y$ is $C^2$ on $\mathbb R^2$. What is the most you can say about $h=\frac{\partial g}{\partial x}=\tfrac73x^{4/3}y$ on $\mathbb R^2$?
options: $h$ is $C^1$ but not $C^2$.
$h$ is $C^2$, like $g$.
$h$ is continuous but not $C^1$.
$h$ is discontinuous on the line $x=0$.

questions.question: Let $f\colon E\to\mathbb R^k$, where $E\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ is open. Write $Df(x)$ for its total derivative, represented by a $k\times2$ matrix; continuity of this matrix map means continuity of all entries. Which condition is equivalent to $f$ being $C^1$ on $E$?
options: $f$ is differentiable at every point of $E$.
$f$ is continuous on $E$ and has all directional derivatives.
All first partials exist and are continuous along each coordinate line in $E$.
$f$ is differentiable on $E$ and $x\mapsto Df(x)$ is continuous.

questions.question: All second-order partials of $f\colon\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R$ exist everywhere and are continuous at $(0,0)$. Every disc centred at $(0,0)$ nevertheless contains a point where some second-order partial is discontinuous. Which conclusion follows?
options: $f$ is $C^2$ on some neighbourhood of $(0,0)$, and its mixed partials agree at $(0,0)$.
$f$ is $C^2$ on no neighbourhood of $(0,0)$, but its mixed partials agree at $(0,0)$.
$f$ is $C^2$ on no neighbourhood of $(0,0)$, and its mixed partials may differ at $(0,0)$.
$f$ is $C^2$ on no neighbourhood of $(0,0)$, but its mixed partials must agree everywhere.

questions.question: Let $f(x,y)=x^2y/(x^2+y^2)$ for $(x,y)\ne(0,0)$ and $f(0,0)=0$. For the unit vector $u=(1,1)/\sqrt2$, define $D_uf(0,0)=\lim_{t\to0}[f(tu)-f(0,0)]/t$. What does comparison with the coordinate partials show?
options: $f$ is $C^1$: both coordinate partials vanish at the origin.
$f$ is $C^1$: directional derivatives exist in every direction.
$f$ is not $C^1$: $D_uf(0,0)\ne\nabla f(0,0)\cdot u$
$f$ is not $C^1$: its values on the diagonal do not approach zero.

questions.question: Let $f(x,y)=q(x)+y^2$, where $q(x)=x^4\sin(1/x)$ for $x\ne0$ and $q(0)=0$. Here $q'(0)=q''(0)=0$, and for $x\ne0$, $q''(x)=12x^2\sin(1/x)-6x\cos(1/x)-\sin(1/x)$. What can be said about $f$ on $\mathbb R^2$?
options: Its second-order partials all exist, but it is not $C^2$.
It is $C^2$, because its second-order partials all exist.
It is $C^2$, because its two mixed partials agree everywhere.
It is not $C^1$, because $q''$ oscillates near zero.
